question:
Consider the pytest test class `TestRunTrialExceptionMix` in `optuna_qa/optimize_run_trial_m5_exceptions/files/testcase.py`. Run ALL test methods of this class (the whole class, e.g. `pytest optuna_qa/optimize_run_trial_m5_exceptions/files/testcase.py::TestRunTrialExceptionMix`), and consider the function `optuna.study._optimize._run_trial` defined in `optuna/study/_optimize.py` (it is reached indirectly via `optuna.study.Study.optimize`).

Count how many times exceptions of each type are OBSERVED in the frame of `_run_trial`, aggregated over the whole run: over every invocation of `_run_trial` (an invocation is one call of the function) and over every test method of the class.

Observation rule: an exception is observed in the `_run_trial` frame each time either (a) a statement executing in that frame raises it (including an explicit `raise <expr>` statement and a failing `assert`), or (b) it propagates into that frame out of a call made from that frame (e.g. an exception escaping `func(trial)`, `study.ask()` or `_tell_with_warning(...)`; it does not matter how deep in the callee it was originally raised). Each such event counts once. An explicit `raise <expr>` that raises an exception object that was already observed earlier in the same frame counts AGAIN as a new observation. A bare `raise` statement (re-raising the exception currently being handled, with no operand) does NOT count again. Exceptions raised and fully handled inside a callee (never escaping into `_run_trial`) are NOT observed. Being caught by an `except` clause of `_run_trial` does not undo an observation. Only the `_run_trial` frame itself matters; observations in other frames are ignored.

Exception type naming: use the bare `type(exc).__name__` for built-in exception classes (e.g. `OSError`, never `builtins.OSError`), and `type(exc).__module__ + "." + type(exc).__qualname__` for all other classes (e.g. `optuna.exceptions.DuplicatedStudyError`).

Answer format: a JSON object with a single key `exception_type_counts` whose value is a list of objects `{"exception_type": <str>, "count": <int>}`, one object per distinct exception type observed at least once (types never observed are omitted; no zero counts). `count` is the total number of observations of that type (totals over all invocations and all test methods, not the number of distinct invocations or tests). Sort the list by `exception_type` ascending using plain Python string ordering (code-point order); exception_type values are unique so no further tie-break is needed.
